protocols.title: Charge a marker signal (Dogs Trust pattern)
protocols.intendedOutcome: Dog shows clear anticipation (orientation toward handler/treats) immediately after marker with no behaviour requirement.
inappropriateWhen: Dog is too stressed or fearful to accept food in the current environment
Dog has medical dietary restrictions without veterinarian-approved alternatives
protocols.environment: Indoors or calm area; minimal distractions for initial charging.
protocols.baselineAssessment: Owner confirms dog will eat offered treats in the training location.

steps.instruction: Choose one marker (calm verbal word such as 'yes', clicker, whistle, or visual signal for deaf dogs) and use it consistently in tone and form.
steps.rewardTiming: Deliver treat immediately after each marker.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog orients toward handler or treats within one second of marker on repeated trials.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Use higher-value treats; reduce environmental stimulation; increase distance from distractions.
failureModes: Marker word used in daily speech causing confusion

steps.instruction: Repeat marker then treat pairing multiple times in a short session until dog visibly anticipates food after the marker alone.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat within 1–2 seconds of marker on every repetition during charging phase.
steps.progressCriteria: Anticipatory response to marker without requiring body movement cue.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Shorten sessions; pause if dog disengages.
failureModes: Gaps between marker and treat too long

steps.instruction: Begin teaching new behaviours only after charging criterion met; maintain rule that marker is always followed by reward during learning phase.
steps.rewardTiming: Marker marks exact behaviour instant; reward follows immediately.
steps.progressCriteria: Stable anticipation across at least two sessions.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Re-charge marker in easier environment if anticipation fades.

reinforcementOptions: Social praise if calm enough not to disrupt learning
protocols.generalisationMaintenance: Re-charge briefly after long breaks or highly stressful events if marker value drops.
safetyPrecautions: Do not train on full stomach if dog prone to vomiting with excitement—adjust timing
protocols.appProgressionNotes: Good Dog session rep counts are provisional until in-app testing; sources do not specify universal repetition numbers.

protocols.title: Recall training — three-step progression (Dogs Trust)
protocols.intendedOutcome: Dog returns to handler promptly on one recall cue in progressively distracting environments.
inappropriateWhen: Dog showing severe fear, aggression, or panic outdoors without qualified behaviour support plan
Unsafe environment (traffic, unfenced livestock) without long-line or secure area
equipment: Household-agreed recall word and visual cue
protocols.environment: Start indoors, garden, or enclosed space; later generalise with long line outdoors.
protocols.baselineAssessment: Owner can get name response reliably in low distraction settings before adding recall cue.

steps.instruction: Establish reliable name response, then introduce one short recall cue (e.g. 'come' or 'here') plus optional open-arms visual signal; ensure all household members use the same cues.
steps.rewardTiming: Reward not applicable until recall occurs; during name work reward orientation to name.
steps.progressCriteria: Consistent name orientation in low distraction before recall cue added.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Return to name-only games; reduce distance and distractions.
failureModes: Different cues used by family members

steps.instruction: In enclosed space, get attention with name, give recall cue, step away; reward generously with praise and treats when dog arrives; use happy voice and welcoming body language even if response is slow.
steps.rewardTiming: Reward immediately on arrival; use especially high value rewards after disengaging from interesting stimuli.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog willingly approaches from increasing short distances indoors/enclosed garden.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Shorten distance; increase treat value; reduce distractions.
failureModes: Ending walk or scolding on return

steps.instruction: Increase distance and distractions gradually; let dog move away before cueing recall; use long line on harness for safety; if ignore occurs stay calm, guide gently with long line without pulling toward you, or collect dog; reward high-value when dog returns without extra guidance.
steps.rewardTiming: High-value reward on voluntary return; intermittent rewards after skill stabilises.
steps.progressCriteria: Reliable recalls on long line with moderate distractions before off-lead in open spaces.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Reduce distraction level; increase distance slowly; use secure fields.

reinforcementOptions: Access to sniff/explore as life reward after successful recall
protocols.generalisationMaintenance: Practice regularly even if dog usually on lead; occasional high-value rewards to maintain motivation.
stopConditions: Repeated failure without improvement—refer to qualified trainer/behaviourist
Dog escaping harness or long line—fix equipment before continuing
safetyPrecautions: Off-lead in open spaces only when confident recall is reliable
Collar ID tag and microchip compliance per UK guidance (verify legally current)
Use harness and long line; do not pull dog toward handler on line
referralRequirements: Persistent running away without improvement → qualified trainer or behaviourist (Dogs Trust)
protocols.reviewReason: Pilot export approved with assessment-metrics.json and safe-002 sanitization (review-001 resolved).
protocols.appProgressionNotes: Five-second inter-cue interval taken from Dogs Trust; Good Dog should label as source-based guidance not research constant.

protocols.title: Teach sit with food lure (RSPCA six-step outline)
protocols.intendedOutcome: Dog sits on verbal cue 'sit' with hindquarters on ground.
inappropriateWhen: Orthopaedic pain when sitting—seek veterinary assessment first
protocols.environment: Quiet room with minimal distractions initially.
protocols.baselineAssessment: Dog can stand comfortably and follow food lure with nose.

steps.instruction: With dog standing, hold treat near nose.
steps.rewardTiming: No reward until sit occurs in later steps.
failureModes: Lure held too high causing jump

steps.instruction: Move hand in arc over head so dog follows treat; as head rises, bottom goes to floor; praise and treat the instant sit happens.
steps.progressCriteria: Bottom contacts floor following lure arc.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Smaller arc; reward partial sits only if shaping intentionally.
failureModes: Backing up instead of sitting—train with wall behind

steps.rewardTiming: Treat each successful sit during acquisition.

steps.instruction: Add verbal cue 'sit' as dog moves into sit, not before movement.
steps.rewardTiming: Treat on completed sit after cue timed correctly.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog sits when lure used with correctly timed verbal cue.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Delay adding verbal cue until lure reliable.

steps.progressCriteria: Sit begins without excessive lure dependence.
steps.easierIfStruggling: Fade lure gradually—not specified numerically by RSPCA.

steps.instruction: Use an 'okay' or release cue to mark end of exercise.
steps.rewardTiming: Optional release reward per owner choice.
steps.progressCriteria: Dog waits until release after sit when trained for duration separately.

protocols.generalisationMaintenance: Practice in new rooms and with mild distractions after quiet-room success.
protocols.appProgressionNotes: Lure fade criteria are provisional for Good Dog UX.
